newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh sees no private investment in sugar.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh sees no private investment in sugar.

text.p: Low yields, high costs and a long harvest mean losses for Bangladesh sugar producers, little private interest in the industry and trouble for the government in maintaining 16 mills, industry officials said on Thursday.
But the good news is Bangladesh expects to produce 215,000 tonnes of sugar in calendar 1997 against 184,000 tonnes in 1996, when both drought and excessive rain hurt sugarcane yield.
"We expect higher sugar production as the climate seems moderately good this year," said Showkat Ali, chairman of state-run Bangladesh Sugar and Food Industries Corp.
Corporation officials said the government planned to import 150,000 tonnes of sugar in 1997 to meet the annual requirement of 350,000 tonnes and to create a buffer stock.
"Sugarcane yield is lowest and sugar content is minimum in Bangladesh. Besides, there is am irrigation problem," Ali said.
The per acre yield is 20 tonnes of cane, and the sugar content is around eight percent, according to official figures.
"The duration of the croping period (12-14 months) and the irrigation problem are discouraging growers to go for sugarcane cultivation," he said.

Sugarcane cultivation is concentrated mainly in the country's north and northwest. "In the south where there is sufficient rainfall, the growers go for short-duration cropping such as the rice," Ali said.

There are about 600,000 families engaged in sugarcane production. "At least five million Bangladeshis are directly or indirectly involved in sugar production process. This is because of fragmented lands," Ali said.
It also is one reason why there is little private sector interest in the industry.
"It's very difficult for the private sector to handle such a huge number of growers," he said.
Industry sources said efforts to privatise the sugar mills had been in limbo because of the losses in the sector.

"Even 15 percent of Zeal Bangla Sugar Mills shares, offered to its employees, have not yet been subscribed," said one corporation official. He said 34 percent of shares of the listed company had been sold through the Dhaka Stock Exchange.
The government planned to sell up to 10 percent of the shares of Carew & Co, a sugar company that has a subsidiary that produces liqours.

Corporation officials said the government wanted to privatise three more sugar mills, set up two new ones and modernise six others. It is seeking foreign help, especially from China and Pakistan, to modernise the existing mills.

Losses by the sugar mills jumped to more than $200 million in fiscal 1992/93 (July-June) with all 16 companies in the red. The losses fell to less than $20 million 1993/94 but rose to about $75 million in 1995/96, according to official figures.
Officials said the government had prepared tender schedules for importing 150,000 tonnes of white crystal sugar in 1997.

But traders said thousands of tonnes of sugar were being smuggled into Bangladesh from neighboring India. Smuggled Indian sugar now sells for 24 taka (56 cents) per kg against 34 taka (80 cents) for local sugar.

The per capita annual sugar consuption in Bangladesh is only three kilograms, one of the lowest in the world. Nearly half of Bangladesh's nearly 120 million people live below the poverty level. The country's per capita annual income is about $260.
